name: Faster Base64 Encoding/Decoding using AVX2 (base64simd)
workload: Single-threaded encoding/decoding of byte streams to/from base64 on a Skylake processor, measured in CPU cycles per input byte, vs Google Chrome's base64 codec
claimed_speedup: ~10x faster encoding, ~7x faster decoding vs state-of-the-art scalar codec; ~0.25 cycles/input byte for long inputs on AVX2
hardware: Intel Skylake @ 3.4 GHz, 32 kB L1 data cache
stars_or_usage: 172 stars; underlying algorithm merged into simdutf (Node.js, Chromium, WebKit)
tradeoffs: Requires x86 SSE/AVX2/AVX-512 or ARM NEON; falls back to scalar on unsupported CPUs; strict base64 validation
caveats: Numbers are from the published paper's own benchmark (Table VI), single-threaded and Intel-only; ARM NEON variants added later without the same full methodology
found_via: crossref.org bibliographic search 'Faster Base64 Encoding and Decoding using AVX2 Instructions' -> arXiv:1704.00605 (Muła & Lemire, ACM Trans. on the Web 2018, DOI 10.1145/3132709)

name: Turbo Base64 (TurboBase64)
workload: Single-thread encode/decode with error checking of 1MB, 50,000B and 10,000B buffers on AMD Ryzen 9 7950X and Intel i7-9700K
claimed_speedup: AVX-512VBMI: 77,619 MB/s encode / 76,716 MB/s decode on Ryzen 9 7950X vs Google Chrome base64 baseline ~2,541/4,289 MB/s (~10-18x); AVX2 tb64v256: 32,794 MB/s encode on i7-9700K, faster than aklomp/base64 and lemire/fastbase64 AVX2 variants in the same table
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 7950X @ 4.50 GHz, DDR5-6000 CL30; Intel i7-9700K @ 3.6 GHz
tradeoffs: GPL-3.0 copyleft (commercial license available); JIT scalar/SSE/AVX/AVX2/AVX512 dispatch adds code complexity
caveats: Benchmark run and published by the project author (first-party), but CPU model, compiler, and code are all fully disclosed and public, meeting tier A on methodology alone
found_via: HN Algolia query 'SIMD base64' -> powturbo Show HN threads for Turbo Base64

name: aklomp/base64 (SIMD Base64 C99 library)
workload: Encode/decode of a 1MB buffer, single-threaded, in a third-party shootout (Turbo-Base64's own benchmark) on an Intel i7-9700K
claimed_speedup: AVX2 variant (b64avx2): 26,153 MB/s encode / 22,515 MB/s decode vs Google Chrome base64 baseline 2,541/4,289 MB/s (~10x encode, ~5x decode) (derived from page data)
tradeoffs: C99 API; OpenMP option for extra parallel speedup; no NEON tuning as aggressive as competitors
caveats: Speedup numbers come from a competing project's (Turbo-Base64) benchmark table rather than aklomp's own README, though CPU/compiler are disclosed there
found_via: gh api graphql search 'base64 simd in:name,description,readme'; cross-checked in Turbo-Base64 README benchmark table

name: fastbase64 (Klomp/Muła/Lemire AVX2 codec, predecessor of simdutf base64)
workload: Encode/decode of a 1MB buffer, single-threaded, in a third-party shootout (Turbo-Base64's own benchmark) on an Intel i7-9700K
claimed_speedup: fb64avx2: 23,686 MB/s encode / 21,231 MB/s decode vs Google Chrome base64 baseline 2,541/4,289 MB/s (~9x encode, ~5x decode) (derived from page data)
stars_or_usage: 445 stars; repo is archived, project's own README states it is superseded by simdutf
tradeoffs: Archived/read-only repository; no further support, algorithm lives on inside simdutf
caveats: Numbers are from a third-party comparison table (Turbo-Base64), not the repo's own benchmark page; repo is explicitly deprecated by its author
found_via: Cross-referenced from Turbo-Base64 README shootout table

name: vb64 (Rust std::simd Base64 codec)
workload: Encode/decode benchmark vs the `base64` crate on an AMD Zen 2 machine with AVX2
claimed_speedup: Decoding 2-2.5x faster, encoding 1.2-1.5x faster than the `base64` crate with AVX2; roughly even/worse with only SSSE3
stars_or_usage: 90 stars; companion code to the 441-point HN thread 'Designing a SIMD Algorithm from Scratch' (mcyoung.xyz)
tradeoffs: Requires Rust nightly for std::simd; Rust-only, no C API
caveats: No exact CPU model given (only 'Zen 2 machine'); first-party blog-post-grade benchmark, no raw throughput numbers, only ratios
found_via: HN Algolia query 'SIMD base64' -> mcyoung.xyz 'Designing a SIMD Algorithm from Scratch' -> linked vb64 repo

name: simdutf Base64 (WHATWG forgiving-base64, ignorable-character SIMD decoding)
workload: SIMD decoding of base64 strings containing ignorable ASCII whitespace (WHATWG forgiving-base64), vs traditional/scalar decoding, on x64 and ARM
claimed_speedup: Paper abstract states the novel functions "multiply the base64 decoding speed compared to traditional methods"; exact factor not confirmed by us (see caveats)
stars_or_usage: 1,979 stars; used in Node.js, WebKit/Safari, Chromium, Ladybird, Bun, Cloudflare Workers, Ghostty
tradeoffs: C++17 library; base64 feature can be compiled out (--with-base64); safe variants have measurable overhead on whitespace-heavy short inputs per the project's own README
caveats: The Authorea preprint PDF (Lemire, 'Base64 Decoding with Ignorable Characters using SIMD instructions', 2025, DOI 10.22541/au.175692137.72576748/v1) was behind a bot-check page and could not be fetched this session; only the Crossref-hosted abstract was confirmed, so hardware/compiler/exact multiplier are unverified and the tier is capped at C
found_via: crossref.org bibliographic search 'Faster Base64 Encoding and Decoding' surfaced the related 2025 Lemire preprint

name: fast-crc32 (corsix) — novel CRC32/CRC32C SIMD kernels
workload: CRC32/CRC32C checksum of buffers, single core, across x86_64 (SSE/AVX-512+VPCLMULQDQ) and aarch64 (NEON+crypto), vs Chromium's zlib crc32_simd.c and the author's own prior crc32c_4k implementations
claimed_speedup: Apple M1: 9.6% faster (77.55->85.05 GB/s); Cascade Lake: 25% faster (25.32->31.55 GB/s); Ice Lake: 56% faster (41.00->63.98 GB/s); Sapphire Rapids: 19% faster (81.68->97.30 GB/s)
compiler_and_flags: per-variant gcc-equivalent flags stated, e.g. -msse4.2 -mpclmul (sse), -mavx512f -mavx512vl -mvpclmulqdq (avx512_vpclmulqdq), -march=armv8-a+crypto+crc (aarch64 neon)
hardware: Apple M1; Intel Xeon (Cascade Lake, Ice Lake @2.6GHz, Sapphire Rapids Platinum 8481C @2.7GHz); AMD Zen3/Zen4 (exact /proc/cpuinfo dumps included in README)
tradeoffs: Code-generator based (terse syntax -> generate.c produces per-architecture C); some variants need very recent CPU extensions (VPCLMULQDQ, SHA3/EOR3)
caveats: Baseline is the prior state-of-the-art SIMD CRC32/CRC32C (zlib's Chromium-vectorized code and the author's own earlier work), not a naive scalar table-based CRC32 loop, though it directly beats named CRC32/CRC32C incumbents
found_via: gh api graphql search 'crc32 simd pclmulqdq in:name,description,readme'

name: crc-fast (Rust core, C/C++ compatible) — generic SIMD CRC-16/32/64
workload: CRC-32/ISCSI and CRC-32/ISO-HDLC checksum of 1KiB and 1MiB buffers on named cloud/desktop CPUs
claimed_speedup: Up to >220x faster than the scalar `crc` crate (~0.5 GiB/s); e.g. CRC-32/ISCSI on Sapphire Rapids avx512-vpclmulqdq: ~111 GiB/s at 1MiB vs ~0.5 GiB/s baseline
compiler_and_flags: per-row target feature strings given (e.g. avx512-vpclmulqdq, neon-pmull-sha3); exact rustc version/flags not stated
hardware: Intel Sapphire Rapids (EC2 c7i.metal-24xl), AMD Genoa (EC2 c7a.metal-48xl), AWS Graviton4/Graviton2, Apple M3 Ultra, Apple M4 Max
tradeoffs: Rust core with C/C++ FFI bindings provided for non-Rust use; huge aggregate speedup spans many different cloud CPUs rather than one controlled machine
caveats: rustc version/flags not stated in the README table; numbers are first-party but hardware and instruction-set target are itemized per row, meeting tier A on disclosure
found_via: gh api graphql search 'crc32 simd pclmulqdq in:name,description,readme'

name: crc32fast (Rust CRC32 SIMD)
workload: CRC32 (IEEE) checksum throughput, comparing this crate's baseline/pclmulqdq implementations to the `crc` crate
claimed_speedup: baseline impl 1,499 MB/s, pclmulqdq impl 7,314 MB/s vs `crc` crate's 207 MB/s (~7x and ~35x respectively)
stars_or_usage: 338 stars; widely depended upon in the Rust ecosystem (e.g. flate2, png crates)
tradeoffs: Rust-only crate, no C API; runtime CPU feature detection requires std (no_std loses SIMD paths)
caveats: README benchmark table gives no CPU model or compiler flags, so capped at tier C despite the large claimed multiplier
found_via: gh api graphql search 'crc32 simd pclmulqdq in:name,description,readme'

name: fast-hex (SIMD hex encode/decode)
workload: Hex encode/decode of byte buffers using AVX2, vs a scalar hex codec (C++ lib) and vs Node.js's native hex codec (Node module)
claimed_speedup: C++: ~12.5x decoding, ~11.5x encoding over scalar; Node.js module: ~2.1x-12x decoding, ~5.5x encoding over Node's built-in hex
compiler_and_flags: requires AVX2 (-march=haswell / MSVC /arch:AVX2); exact flags/CPU used to produce the quoted ratios not stated
tradeoffs: No input validation by default (author notes this as a possible future PR); requires Haswell-or-later AVX2, no runtime fallback dispatch mentioned
caveats: Benchmark numbers are ratios only; no CPU model, compiler version, or raw throughput figures published, so capped at tier C
found_via: gh api graphql search 'hex simd encode decode in:name,description,readme' (arXiv/crossref turned up no hex-specific SIMD papers)
